title: Chapter 14: Nobody's Daughter
content: The ferry crosses at seven with nobody in it, which has not happened since 1975, and Wren runs the drum by hand the whole way because the motor has been growling since August and she is not going to let it fail with a boat under her.

Thirty-eight turns of the drum, two hundred feet of water, and the west ramp comes up out of the fog like a thing she is being shown for the first time. She ties off, checks the pin, and walks up Mill Street with her collar up.

The county paper is one room over the pharmacy, up a stair with a handrail worn pale in the middle. The window has the name in gold leaf that has been repaired in three places: KETTLER COUNTY COURIER. Founded 1889. Under that, in smaller letters, a motto somebody chose a hundred years ago and nobody has had the nerve to change: PRINTED WHERE THE RIVER RUNS.
Harlan Pike is at the back with a scanner from 1997 and a cup of coffee he has forgotten. He is fifty-two and he has his father's heavy shoulders and none of his father's luck.
"You are early," he says.
"You said seven thirty."
"I said come at seven thirty. I did not think you would."
He lifts a milk crate onto the desk. Cardboard folders stand in it, upright, tabbed in a hand that is not his, and the whole thing smells of the inside of an attic.

"Thirty-two years of clips," he says. "Nineteen ninety-four forward. There is a folder in there with your name on it, and one with your mother's, and one with your grandfather's that I started on the fourteenth of September and have not finished, because I keep writing the same paragraph and crossing it out."
Wren puts her hand on the top folder and does not open it.
"What do you want for it," she says.
"An interview."
"No."
"Twenty minutes. In your kitchen, with the boat behind you."
"No."

"You are the story, Wren. I am not saying that to be cruel. A woman files forty-one forms and the county queues to the street. That is a story. That is the only story this paper has had since the school roof."
"The forty-one are the story."

"Nobody reads forty-one." He says it without apology, which is the thing she likes least and trusts most about him. "They read one. They read a name and a face and a kitchen. Then they read the next one. That is how it works. That is how it has always worked."
"Then print one. Print Owen Pike."
Harlan's hand stops on the crate.

"Owen Pike drowned in 1994," she says. "He was forty-three. He crossed at six twelve in the morning with one soul aboard, and my grandfather wrote the fare in the margin because the man had no change, and eight minutes later the gate opened for silt and the water came up over the landing and took him off the lower bank while he was setting his nets."
Harlan sits down slowly, in the chair he was already standing beside.
"Eight minutes," he says.

"Eight minutes. It is on page two hundred and eleven. There is a pencil note in the margin that says gate six twenty, and the pencil is smeared, because my grandfather wrote it with his thumb on the page."
"He was twenty when it happened," Harlan says. "I was twenty. I was at a dance in Chester. Somebody came in and said there had been an accident at the landing and I said whose."
"You can print that. You do not need me in a kitchen."
"I can print that," he says, "and it will be four inches on page nine, and the man who reads it will say Owen Pike, I remember Owen, and turn the page to the football."
"Then print it on page one."
He looks at her for a while. The scanner hums and stops and the room smells of dust and old toner.
"There is a thing in that crate about your mother," he says. "I want you to hear it from me before you read it. I wrote her obituary in August of 2011. Forty lines. It was set and it never ran."
"Why."

"Because it was killed upstairs. And upstairs was not me." He turns his cup a quarter turn, and does not drink. "I have kept it in the file for fifteen years. It is the only thing in this office I am ashamed of."
Wren picks up the crate. It is heavier than it looks.
"Page one," she says.
"I will think about it."
"Think about it while you set the type."
Harlan almost laughs, and it turns into something else halfway, and he waves her out of the office with the back of his hand.

She ferries back with the crate on the deck between her feet and the fog burning off the water in strips. Two passengers, both of them from the Quill place, both of them silent, both of them paying in ones. The ferry is full of the sound of the drum and nothing else. There are two more crossings before noon and three in the afternoon. In September she ran twenty-two a day. She writes every name in the log and underlines the ones who paid in ones, which is most of them now.

At the house she sets the crate on the kitchen table and puts the kettle on and does not open it. She takes the biscuit tin down from the top of the dresser instead, because she has been putting this off for a week and the crate has made it impossible.
Three letters, folded in three, in her own hand, unsent.
The first is dated the fifteenth of September.

Theo. You left in October and I told myself I did not mind, and that was true for about a year, and then it stopped being true and I never told you that either. I am writing this because you came back with her hand on your arm and you said my name like an apology, and I have spent all day deciding whether a person is allowed to be angry at a man for doing what his family told him to do. I have decided that she is.

Not for leaving. For coming back and standing in the diner and telling me you would look at my file personally, as though a note on a file were the same size as a man. It is not. He is not a file. I am not a file. The river is not a file. I am not going to send this.
The second is dated the twenty-seventh.

Theo. Shorter, because I have started to hear myself. You did not know my grandfather's name until it was typed on a form. That is not a crime. It is a fact about you, and I have been carrying the fact around like a stone in my coat, and the strange part is that I do not want to put it down. I want to hand it to you. I am not going to send this either.
The third is dated today, the tenth of October, and it is on the back of a receipt from the hardware store.
Theo. The river was at the second rung. That is all I have tonight. I am not going to send this one.
She folds them and puts them back in the tin and puts the tin on the dresser, and then she opens the crate.
The morgue is not arranged by year. It is arranged by name, and the names are the ones that kept coming back, and Aubrey has a folder an inch and a half thick.

Inside, on top, a single page, typed on the paper's own letterhead at some point in the nineties and updated by hand ever since. It has no byline and no date and it is written in the voice the paper uses for things it will not argue about.

FILE: AUBREY, E. AND AUBREY, D. AND AUBREY, W.
SUBJECT: crossings and deaths, Mile 9 and Mile 11, Sable River, Kettler County.
HOLDINGS: fourteen clippings. Three photographs. One obituary, unpublished. One correction, unpublished.

1957: ferry franchise transferred to E. Aubrey. Nine passengers, painted on hull. No county inspection on file.
1961: crossing log begun. Prior volume lost to fire, per interview, 1988.
1994: first recorded gate death below Kettler Gate. O. Pike, 43. Cause not certified. No inquest.
2011: D. Aubrey, 32, Mile 11, single vehicle. Cause not certified. No obituary published.
2026: E. Aubrey, 78, Mile 9. Photograph used, page one. Cause pending.
NOTE, 1996: this paper does not print the word drowned in a headline without a coroner's finding. Readers have complained. The rule stands.
Wren reads the note at the bottom twice. That is why. That is the whole architecture of it, in five lines, in a folder, in a crate, over a pharmacy. Not a conspiracy. A style rule.

Then she goes through the clippings. Her grandfather at nineteen with the log under his arm, squinting. The ferry in the flood of 1997 with a tree across the apron. A photograph of the landing in 2011 with three cars parked on it and a man in waders, and she looks at the corner of the frame for a girl and there is no girl in the frame.

The folder with her mother's name in it has four clippings and a proof sheet of the obituary that never ran. Forty lines. It says Dana Marie Aubrey, thirty-two, of Mile 11, and it says she is survived by a daughter, and the daughter's name is spelled right, and somebody has drawn a single line through the whole thing in grease pencil and written HOLD in the margin.
Under the proof sheet is a padded envelope, postmarked Tuesday, in Mars's handwriting, with no note inside and a photocopy of a photocopy, nine pages, stapled twice.
Dana M. Aubrey. 17 August 2011. Form 9, cause line blank, the stub of a word typed and struck through, and in the corner the same stamp she has seen forty-one times.
PENDING.

The sheriff's report is one page. Single vehicle, Route 11 bridge, 11:40 p.m. Road dry. Rail intact, inspected the twenty-second, no defect found. Water fourteen feet at the pier. One occupant. No other vehicle involved. No witnesses.
Next of kin: daughter, Wren Aubrey, age 9, resident of 9 Ferry Lane with E. Aubrey, grandfather.
And under that, in the box marked remarks, a sentence in a young deputy's hand: The child was on the bank at first light. Child was not interviewed.
The routing slip is stapled to the back. Two boxes. Received, District 4, stamped 19 AUG 2011. Reviewed by, blank.
The note is in the margin beside the sentence about the child. Four words and a date and two letters, in a small even hand, in blue ink that has gone grey.
Do not interview the minor.
Wren sits with it. The kettle has boiled and gone cold and boiled again and she has not got up.
She knows the hand. She has seen it on an envelope with her own name on it, in ink, in a house on a bluff, with a brass telescope on the terrace pointed at the gate.
highlight: Alone on the east bank, Wren reads her mother's 2011 file and recognizes the hand that wrote the note in it.
